card.hook: Look up the moment you step in from Little Collins Street: two carved giants are standing guard over a clock, and they hit bells with their arms every hour. Not what you expect above a row of shops, is it?
card.stand_here: Stand just inside the doors at the Little Collins Street end of Royal Arcade, then turn round and look up at Gog and Magog beside Gaunt's Clock. If you're walking in from Bourke Street Mall or Little Collins Street, the middle of the arcade is about 1 minute on foot to the north.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit both giants, the clock and the arch in one go. Then try 1x for a cleaner view, and zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) to get close to the clock face or the carved figures.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the clock, then slide the brightness down a little so the bright glass roof doesn't wash out the carvings.
card.best_time: Aim for just before the top of the hour, when the giants strike the bells. Get there a few minutes early to claim your spot and set up your shot.
card.selfie_here: Stand just below the clock beside Gog and Magog near the Little Collins Street entrance, so you and the arcade's most famous feature share the frame. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone up a bit so the clock sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand back in the middle of the corridor on the black-and-white floor, so you're framed against the arches and glass roof, with the clock behind you if you like.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a shopping arcade and a walk-through for shoppers, so keep moving gently and check the official site before you go for opening times and any access rules.
card.challenge: Can you get both giants perfectly balanced on either side of the clock, just as it's about to strike?
card.good_to_know: Royal Arcade opened in 1870 and is the oldest surviving arcade in Australia. Gog and Magog were added in 1893 and are based on the figures in London's Guildhall. The shopfronts were restored in 2002-04 and painted yellow and white with gilded touches, which is why everything photographs so warmly.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand just inside the doors at the Little Collins Street end of Royal Arcade, then turn round and look up at Gog and Magog beside Gaunt's Clock. If you're walking in from Bourke Street Mall or Little Collins Street, the middle of the arcade is about 1 minute on foot to the north.

card.hook: Walk into Yarra Park and the MCG's floodlights pop up over the trees like giant cricket fans peeking over a fence. It's a big stadium, so give it room in your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Yarra Park, west of the ground near Jolimont station, and turn to look back at the stadium. You'll see the floodlights and stands rising above the trees, with open lawn and paths in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the stands, floodlights and trees all in. Then try 1x for a more natural look. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out the floodlights and roofline above the treetops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the stadium along the upper third with lawn or a path below it, then tap the floodlights and slide a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Pick a day with no match, because the park fills up with parking and crowds on match days. Morning or late afternoon usually gives you softer light.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the bronze Shane Warne statue in Yarra Park, where the MCG fills the background. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tilt up a little so the stadium sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the top of William Barak Bridge while you stand on the parkland in front of the stadium, so the stadium and light towers are framed behind you (dusk works best).
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks can't be taken into the MCG, according to its conditions of entry (January 2025 version, and the rules may change). If you're near the Batman Avenue Overpass on a cricket match day, watch for heavy foot traffic.
card.challenge: Can you get grass, trees and stadium into one shot, with a path leading your eye to the ground, and nobody walking through it?
card.good_to_know: The MCG, known locally as the 'G, is Australia's biggest stadium and holds about 100,000 people. The Melbourne Cricket Club set it up in 1853 on what was a Wurundjeri camping ground. It hosted the world's first Test match in 1877 and the 1956 Olympics opening and closing ceremonies, and today it stages the AFL Grand Final and the Boxing Day Test.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Yarra Park, west of the ground near Jolimont station, and turn to look back at the stadium. You'll see the floodlights and stands rising above the trees, with open lawn and paths in front.

card.hook: Look up and you'll spot a gold crown, a red stripe and a whole lot of blue glass. It looks like a flag, and that's on purpose. Those colours read clearly even on a small phone screen.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map, which sits right at Eureka Tower in Southbank. Find a safe spot outside the building, then step back as far as you can and face the tower.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole tower in from up close. Switch to 1x for the base and the gold bees. From further back, try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the gold crown and the red stripe.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower's straight edges up with them, holding your phone as upright as you can so the tower doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is kinder to the glass than harsh midday light. A clear day shows off the blue and the gold best, and the sun's direction decides which side of the tower lights up.
card.selfie_here: Try the riverside lawns at Birrarung Marr, on the northern bank of the Yarra. Use the front camera at 0.5x, face away from the tower so it sits behind you across the river, and check the angle on the spot. Morell Bridge, a walkers-and-cyclists-only crossing, is a quiet backup.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Princes Bridge to stand on the bridge deck looking west along the Yarra, so the tower lands on the left of the frame with you in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The Melbourne Skydeck on level 88 has an entry fee, so check the official site before you go if you want pictures from inside.
card.challenge: Find the gold bees around the white box at the base, then get them in the bottom of your shot with the tower rising above them.
card.good_to_know: Eureka Tower is 297.3 m tall and officially opened on 11 October 2006. Its design draws on the Eureka Stockade, the 1854 rebellion in the Victorian gold rush. The gold crown stands for the gold, the red stripe for the blood spilt, and the blue glass and white lines for the stockade flag. The Skydeck on level 88 is the highest public viewing floor in a building in the Southern Hemisphere.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map, which sits right at Eureka Tower in Southbank. Find a safe spot outside the building, then step back as far as you can and face the tower.

card.hook: Plot twist: at this spot the art gallery isn't the star, the river is. The gallery sits across the water with its reflections and the nearby towers, and you're photographing the whole scene.
card.stand_here: Stand in Birrarung Marr, on the northern bank of the Yarra, and face south. The National Gallery of Victoria is about 650 m to the south-west across the river, so it'll sit off to one side of your view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the river, the reflections and the towers in together. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to bring the gallery closer. Zoom 0.5x adds lots of riverbank, but the gallery will look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the water along the bottom third so the reflections fill that part of the picture, and keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Go on a calm, bright day, because still water gives the clearest reflections. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the buildings.
card.selfie_here: Head to the glass Water Wall at the St Kilda Road entrance of NGV International, which several guides call the gallery's signature photo spot. Use the front camera, stand in front of the wall, and let the bluestone building fill the frame behind you. Try zoom 0.5x if you want more of it in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand just inside the St Kilda Road entrance and shoot outward, while you stand in front of the Water Wall so both fill the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: Tripods and selfie sticks aren't allowed in the galleries without NGV permission, and flash needs permission too. Photography is welcome in most areas, but temporary exhibitions can restrict it, so check the signs. Birrarung Marr is an open park, but check the official site for closures or works before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the gallery and its wobbly reflection in the water in the same shot, with the horizon dead level?
card.good_to_know: The NGV was founded in 1861 and is Australia's oldest and most visited art museum. The building on this map is NGV International at 180 St Kilda Road, designed by Sir Roy Grounds and opened in 1968. It's clad in bluestone, is on the Victorian Heritage Register, and was redeveloped by Mario Bellini before reopening in 2003.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Birrarung Marr, on the northern bank of the Yarra, and face south. The National Gallery of Victoria is about 650 m to the south-west across the river, so it'll sit off to one side of your view.

card.hook: Picture a long row of old market shopfronts lined up along the pavement, with the 1884 Meat and Fish Hall facade at the end. That's the Vic Market from Elizabeth Street, and it's a lot more photogenic than you'd expect from a place that sells fish.
card.stand_here: Stand on Elizabeth Street, on the pavement outside the market, and face the old market frontage. Walk along until the whole facade fits on your screen.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x if the pavement is narrow and you want the whole facade in one shot. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for signs and rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roofline up with the horizontal lines, and hold your phone level so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Morning, soon after the market opens, is often said to have the best light. The market isn't open every day, so check opening days before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try String Bean Alley inside the market. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x and hold your arm out so the handmade stalls fill the background behind you. We inferred this spot from descriptions of the alley, so check it when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back from the main entrance while you stand under the WELCOME sign.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos and videos are fine, as long as you don't block walkways, traders or market operations.
card.challenge: Take one wide, straight-on shot of the facade, then find three details up close, like a sign, a roofline and a stall awning, and see if your travel companions can guess where they are.
card.good_to_know: The market officially opened in March 1878 and is on both the Victorian Heritage Register and the National Heritage List. It covers more than seven hectares and is the largest open air market in the Southern Hemisphere. It was built over Melbourne's first British burial ground, the Old Melbourne Cemetery, which is a good story to tell while you shoot.

card.hook: Here's a rare treat: a view your phone almost can't get wrong. The Ornamental Lake is so calm and open that there's nothing close by to confuse it, just water, trees and buildings in a neat row.
card.stand_here: Head to Picnic Point on the lakeside of the Ornamental Lake and face across the water towards The Terrace cafe. Check the exact spot on the map when you get close.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the full sweep of lake, trees and buildings. Try 2x to pick out The Terrace across the water. Zoom 0.5x gives you a big sky, but the far bank ends up looking small and distant.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the far bank on the upper third line so the water fills the bottom of the frame, then tap the far bank and slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Pick a calm day for the clearest reflections. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water.
card.selfie_here: Stand lakeside on the Ornamental Lake with the water and its cluster of islands behind you, and use the front camera. Golden hour (the hour around sunset) is recommended here for the light. If roses are your thing, the QVG Rose Garden makes a colourful backdrop in flowering season, though that tip comes from an older blog.
card.rules_and_safety: Visitors taking photos or filming for their own visit don't need a permit at Melbourne Gardens. Drones and kites are prohibited, and styled setups with props, an arch, furniture or amplified sound need a permit and fee. Some areas and lookouts close from time to time, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the waterline dead level on a gridline and wait for a moment with nobody wandering into the shot. Bonus points for a Live Photo that catches the calmest ripples.
card.good_to_know: The Melbourne Gardens cover 38 hectares on the south side of the Yarra River and were founded in 1846. Almost 50,000 plants from about 8,500 species grow here. The Ornamental Lake was shaped around the turn of the 20th century from the old wetland, and the site has been on the Victorian Heritage Register since 1982.

card.hook: Ask a Melburnian where to meet and you'll hear "under the clocks". Stand across the street for a minute and you'll see why: the dome, the tower and the clocks are all in one big, easy-to-read frame, with trams sliding past.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Flinders Street and Swanston Street (south-east corner of the intersection, at the edge of Federation Square) and look west across Swanston Street. The dome and the Swanston Street side of the station fill the frame, with trams crossing in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the dome and the Swanston Street side in one shot. If the building won't fit, tap 0.5x. To pick out the clocks and the arched entrance, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the dome near an upper third line and keep the vertical lines straight.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun lights this side of the building. For an evening shot, come at blue hour once the lights come on, and use night mode if your phone doesn't switch it on itself.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the bench in front of St Paul's Cathedral, diagonally across from the station, which is a popular spot with visitors. Or stand on the front steps right under the clocks. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low so the station sits behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Federation Square forecourt, directly across Flinders Street, while you wait on the front steps under the clocks, so they can fit the whole facade, dome and all, behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the footpaths and keep clear of tram tracks and crossings. Scaffolding sometimes covers part of the front, so check before making a special trip. Inside the station, personal photos are fine without flash, but check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a tram to cross the bottom of your frame without hiding the dome, then tap the shutter button, or take a burst, and pick your best one.
card.good_to_know: The current station was completed in 1909. A railway station opened on this site in 1854 and is described as the oldest in Australia, though that's not the present building. The building has been on the Victorian Heritage Register since 1982, and it's still the busiest station in Victoria.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Flinders Street and Swanston Street (south-east corner of the intersection, at the edge of Federation Square) and look west across Swanston Street. The dome and the Swanston Street side of the station fill the frame, with trams crossing in front.

card.hook: Picture a giant blade of metal slicing up out of a green lawn, with a Victorian palace parked right next door. That's Melbourne Museum, and the old-meets-new clash is the fun part.
card.stand_here: Stand in Carlton Gardens, on the south side of the gardens, and face the museum across the open lawns. Let the grass fill the bottom of your shot and the angled roof lines rise above it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole building with some grass in front. Go to 0.5x if you're close and want the sweep of the canopies, or 2x from further back to pick out the sharp roof lines.

card.hook: Fed Square looks like someone tipped out a box of sharp, shiny shards right across from Flinders Street station, and somehow it works. Your job is to get all those angles and a big slice of sky in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Federation Square at the northwest corner of the square, and face southeast toward the main facade. It's right at the corner of Flinders and Swanston Streets, across the road from Flinders Street station.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x so the whole angular facade and plenty of sky fit in. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched view of one section, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out repeating panels and sharp edges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the vertical edges straight, hold the phone level (tilting up makes the walls lean in), then tap the facade and slide it a touch darker so the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Go in the afternoon, when the panels catch direct light and the shadows get deeper. The plaza can be busy, so take a few shots at 0.5x and wait for a gap, or let a few people into the bottom of the frame to show scale.
card.selfie_here: On the main plaza, stand in front of the giant TV screen with it behind you. Or sit on the steps facing Flinders Street with the square behind you. Use the front camera, and switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, so more of the scene fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography at Fed Square can need a permit from the Melbourne Arts Precinct Corporation, and the rules don't clearly say whether casual phone selfies count. Inside the cultural institutions and cafes, ask the business before you take photos.

card.good_to_know: Fed Square opened on 26 October 2002. It covers about 3.2 hectares and is built over busy railway lines. It cost about $467 million, over four times the first estimate.

card.hook: Here's a fun trick at the Shrine of Remembrance: you get two completely different photos from one visit. One is the city skyline rising out of the gardens, the other is that big stepped stonework above the parkland.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, which marks the Shrine itself in Kings Domain. For the skyline, go through the building to the upper Balcony around the rooftop terrace and face out over the city. For the outdoor view, climb the forecourt steps and face the skyline across the parkland, with the Shrine behind you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole skyline. Try zoom 0.5x to fit in more of the terrace and gardens. Then use zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out individual towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, and keep a bit of garden in the foreground so the skyline has some depth.
card.best_time: The Balcony is only open during visiting hours, so check the official site before you go. Late afternoon is a good bet for softer light, and the forecourt steps are open at any time.
card.selfie_here: Try the Shrine of Remembrance approach steps. Use the front camera, stand on the steps with the building behind you, and tip the phone up a little so the stonework fits over your shoulder. A travel guide calls the steps a classic photo stop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the forecourt facing the entrance, or partway down the approach steps looking up at the building, while you pose on the steps.
card.rules_and_safety: Only handheld cameras are allowed on and within the Shrine monument, including the courtyards and the Balcony, so keep your phone in your hand. Photography isn't allowed in the galleries. If there's a wreath-laying or ceremony, keep clear and don't photograph it or pose for celebratory shots nearby.
card.challenge: Take a few frames from the steps and a few from the Balcony, then see if your friends can believe they're from the same place.
card.good_to_know: The Shrine was built to honour Victorians who served in World War I, and today it's a memorial to all Australians who have served in any war. Two veteran architects, Phillip Hudson and James Wardrop, designed its stepped, classical shape, drawing on the Parthenon and the ancient tomb at Halicarnassus. It was dedicated on 11 November 1934.

card.hook: Imagine a whole city block of grand stone, with a sloping lawn out front and trams rattling past. State Library Victoria is a great place to practise photographing buildings on your phone, because the walls hand you strong lines.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the library's Swanston Street front, and face the building. Then walk back along the street until the whole portico fits in your screen.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the full width of the building and the portico, then switch to 1x for a more natural look. Try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for carvings, columns and rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines so the building stands up straight.
card.best_time: Our notes don't name a perfect hour, so go when the stonework is nicely lit. If the sky is bright and the front looks dull, tap the stonework and slide it a bit darker to bring the detail back.
card.selfie_here: Outside, stand on the sloped front lawn facing Swanston Street, with the columned portico behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the building fits over your shoulder. Inside, the 6th-floor balcony of the Dome Galleries gives you the dome as your backdrop, but check that level 6 is open before you go.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Swanston Street, opposite the forecourt, while you stand on the forecourt lawn so the whole facade fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is handheld only, so no tripods and no flash. Don't photograph staff or other visitors without their consent, and keep your phone on silent in the La Trobe Reading Room. On the balcony, never rest your phone on the balustrade or lean over it, because a drop would land on people working below. Indoor photo rules can change, so check before you raise your phone.
card.challenge: Snap one shot where every column is dead straight against a gridline, then try to get yourself in it too.
card.good_to_know: The library was established in 1854 as the Melbourne Public Library, which makes it Australia's oldest public library and one of the first free libraries in the world. The portico was added in 1870, and the Domed Reading Room opened in 1913. Its skylights were hidden from 1959 and revealed again in 2003, and the collection includes Ned Kelly's armour.

card.zoom: Start at 1x so the pond, the facade and the dome all fit in one frame. Then try 2x or 5x to pick out the dome (higher zooms depend on your phone). Use 0.5x only if you walk up to the entrance steps and want the whole front in view.

card.hook: Most old buildings try to look welcoming. This one is a wall of dark bluestone with small, severe openings, and it looks properly dramatic even on a dull day.
card.stand_here: Head for Russell Street in central Melbourne, near the corner with La Trobe Street, and stand on the footpath in front of the Old Melbourne Gaol's front entrance. Face the gaol so you can take in the frontage and a bit of the street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get a good length of the frontage in one shot. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the stone texture and small details. Use 0.5x only if you get close to the walls and want to show how tall they are.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the top of the wall up with a horizontal line so it doesn't lean, then tap the stone and slide it a touch darker so the bluestone keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, or on a bright, slightly cloudy day. The stone shows off its texture without harsh glare.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the gaol's front entrance, with the stone walls and iron gates behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit higher so the walls fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand back on the Russell Street footpath in front of the entrance so the whole stone building fits, while you stand at the front entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: If you go inside, photo rules may differ, so check the official site first and follow signs and staff directions. Photography isn't allowed during the Hangman's Night Tour.
card.challenge: Find the smallest, grimmest-looking opening in the wall and frame it so it looks like it's staring right back at you.
card.good_to_know: The Old Melbourne Gaol worked as a prison from 1845 until 1924, and building began in 1839. By 1864 the perimeter wall and gaol were complete, filling an entire city block. 133 people were hanged here, including the bushranger Ned Kelly in November 1880. Today it's a museum telling the stories of prisoners and staff.

card.hook: Picture a path that runs away from you under a roof of elm leaves, with a tree on each side like a guard of honour. That's the Fitzroy Gardens shot, and in autumn the roof turns gold.
card.stand_here: Stand in Fitzroy Gardens at one end of the central elm avenue, then walk east along the path to find it. Face down the path and stand in the middle so both sides match.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the whole avenue and canopy fit. If your phone has 2x, try it too, because it squeezes the trees together and makes the avenue look longer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the path on the centre line, and crouch so the path leads further into the picture.
card.best_time: Go in autumn, March to May, when the elms turn gold. Early morning is best for softer light under the trees.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooden bridge beside the Boy on the Turtle pond in the north part of the gardens, where the plantings around the pond fill the frame behind you. For a cleaner backdrop, use the lawn beside the white-pillared Rotunda (the Temple of the Winds). Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it to fit more garden in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the paved area in front of the Conservatory, near the statue and fountain, and step back far enough that the whole building fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Paths or areas can close for seasonal work, so check the City of Melbourne site before you go. Check the Conservatory is open too.
card.challenge: Take your avenue shot, then spot the gold leaves and take one more with a single leaf in the foreground. Bonus points if nobody walks through the frame.
card.good_to_know: Fitzroy Gardens is a Victorian-era park of about 26 hectares, set aside as public gardens in 1848. The elm avenues were planted as shady walking routes, and together they happen to form a pattern like the Union Jack. The park also has Cooks' Cottage, a conservatory, a lake and a model Tudor village.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole spire and the buildings around it into one upward shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to home in on the lattice pattern.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the spire up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Dusk and after dark are especially striking, when the spire is lit up. Use night mode then, and keep your phone steady. In daylight, a clear sky gives the cleanest background.
card.selfie_here: Try the footpath on Princes Bridge over the Yarra, a classic Melbourne spot where the spire and the river both fill the view. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the spire over your shoulder. We haven't confirmed which way to face, so turn around until the spire and river both fit behind you.
card.ask_someone: On the Princes Bridge footpath, ask a passer-by to take your photo with the spire in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed outside and in the foyer of Hamer Hall, but not during performances. Selfie sticks are not allowed inside the AMPA exhibition space in Hamer Hall. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot showing the spire rising from the buildings, then one tight shot of just the lattice. Can your friends guess it's the same spire?
card.good_to_know: Sir Roy Grounds planned the complex, and the masterplan was approved in 1960. The spire got its lightning conductor rod in 1981, and the original idea was a spire 115 m tall. Hamer Hall opened in 1982 and the Theatres Building in 1984. Much of the centre is built underground.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go round to the rear of Arts Centre Melbourne, between Hamer Hall and the Theatres Building, and stand right under the spire. The phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face up and point your phone at the spire.

card.hook: Trams rattle across, cyclists weave through the walkers, and behind it all the glass towers stand over a bridge that's older than almost everything around it. Princes Bridge is busy all day, but from the right bank it looks wonderfully calm.
card.stand_here: Stand on Southbank Promenade, on the south bank of the Yarra near Hamer Hall, a little upstream of the bridge. Face north, and the bridge sits in front of you with the city towers rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the arches, the river and the skyline all fit in one frame. Then try zoom 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. If your phone has zoom 2x to 5x, use it to pick out the towers behind the bridge.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the bridge along the lower third so the towers fill the top, and keep your phone level so the bridge rail doesn't slope.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise or blue hour. Calm mornings and evenings can turn the river into a mirror. At dusk, use night mode and tuck your elbows against your body or a railing to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to Flinders Walk on the Federation Square side, at the steps or the lift. Use the front camera, turn so the bridge is behind you, and look up at it from the lower level so the ornate structure fills the space over your shoulder. Try 0.5x if your phone offers it on the front camera.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the riverside path near Hamer Hall, slightly upstream, while you stand between them and the bridge so the towers rise behind it.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is busy, so keep to the pavement and stay out of the tram tracks. Never set up on or beside the tracks. The bridge and promenade are free, but check the official site before you go in case of works or event closures.
card.challenge: Switch on Live Photo and catch a tram crossing the bridge, then see if you can sneak yourself into the corner of the frame.
card.good_to_know: The bridge you see today opened on 4 October 1888, and it's been on the Victorian Heritage Register since 1982. It stands on the site of one of the city's oldest river crossings, and some of the stone from the earlier 1850 bridge was reused in it. Look for the bluestone piers and cast-iron detail against the glass towers.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Southbank Promenade, on the south bank of the Yarra near Hamer Hall, a little upstream of the bridge. Face north, and the bridge sits in front of you with the city towers rising behind it.

card.hook: Back in the 1890s, Melburnians strolled along Collins Street just to be seen, and they called it "doing the block". Stand outside this arcade today and you can see why they bothered: the frontage looks barely changed from old photos.
card.stand_here: Stand on the footpath in front of the Collins Street entrance of Block Arcade, facing north towards the ornate six-storey frontage. Put the doorway in the middle of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the frontage and doorway. If the footpath is too tight to fit all six storeys, tap 0.5x. Try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the fancy details up high.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and keep your phone upright, so the doorway and walls stay nice and straight.
card.best_time: There's no special hour for this one, but it gets busy with shoppers around midday. An earlier or quieter part of the day should give you a clearer view.
card.selfie_here: Head inside to the octagonal rotunda, where the arcade bends, and stand under the central glass dome. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold it a bit low so the dome fills the space over your shoulder. The mosaic-tiled main walkway also makes a good backdrop if you want the floor in the shot.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the Collins Street entrance (282 Collins St) and ask a passer-by to frame you with the arcade's entrance behind you, then check on the screen that it fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos inside the arcade are generally fine, but professional or commercial shoots may need permission from arcade management or shop owners. It's an indoor shopping space, so check the official site for opening times and photo rules before you go.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice: once of the frontage from the footpath, then once of the mosaic floor under the dome, and see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: Block Arcade was built between 1891 and 1893 and designed by Twentyman & Askew. The grand opening was on 7 October 1893. The frontage is described as one of Australia's best surviving examples of Victorian Mannerist architecture.

card.hook: Everyone charges straight for the grand front steps of Parliament House, and then spends ten minutes dodging wedding parties and tour groups. Here's a calmer way in.
card.stand_here: Stand in Parliament Gardens, the little triangular garden beside the building between Spring Street and Albert Street. The building is to the south of you, so face that way and you'll see it from the side with the fountain and statues in front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the side view of the building. Go to 0.5x to squeeze the fountain, statues and building into one shot, and keep the building away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the columns and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines so the building stands up straight.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light tends to flatter the stonework. Weekday daytimes can be busy with tour groups, so check for events before you go.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, climb to the top of the front steps and stand between the central columns with the building behind you. The Spring Street side gives you a wide city view too. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold your arm out a bit so the columns frame you.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the Bourke Street side at the Exhibition Street corner and shoot east up Bourke Street, while you pose up the street with Parliament House filling the end of the view.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine in public areas for personal use, but restrictions can apply inside the chambers or during events. There's no stopping or parking directly in front of Parliament House, so don't plan on using a vehicle in your photo. Check the official site before you go, as access to the building, steps and tours can change.
card.challenge: Get the fountain or a statue in the foreground, then see if you can make the whole building look like it's peeking over its shoulder.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1855, and the first session in the new chambers opened on 25 November 1856. The building has never been finished, and the dome that was planned for it is one of Melbourne's best-known unbuilt features. From 1901 to 1927 it also housed the national Parliament, while Melbourne was the temporary capital of Australia.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Parliament Gardens, the little triangular garden beside the building between Spring Street and Albert Street. The building is to the south of you, so face that way and you'll see it from the side with the fountain and statues in front.

card.hook: A tram rattles past, and right behind it a row of pointed stone spires shoots up above the traffic. It's a lovely clash of old and busy, and you get it all in one go.
card.stand_here: Stand at the edge of Federation Square, facing the Flinders and Swanston Streets intersection. The cathedral is across Flinders Street to the north-west, about 170 m away, so face north-west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the facade, spires and trams all in one frame. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the spires and stonework. Save 0.5x for when you want lots of street, but the spires will lean and look smaller.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the spires with an upright line so they don't lean, then put the facade in the top half and let a tram or the street fill the bottom.
card.best_time: Go when the street is a bit quieter and the light is soft. Wires and trees can get in the way, so take a few shots from slightly different spots instead of relying on one.
card.selfie_here: Try the corner beside Flinders Street Station, opposite the cathedral. One guide recommends it for portraits, but it isn't confirmed that the cathedral shows behind you, so use the front camera, try 0.5x, and check the screen for spires over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the Federation Square side of Flinders Street, across from the cathedral, and ask a passer-by to take the shot so the whole neo-Gothic building fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the footpaths, never stand on tram tracks or at tram stops, and cross only at the signalled crossings. Inside, photos need a permit from the cathedral shop, no flash is allowed, and photography is off during services and weddings.
card.challenge: Wait for a tram to glide through the bottom of your frame with the spires above it, then use a Live Photo to pick your favourite moment afterwards.
card.good_to_know: English architect William Butterfield designed the cathedral, and it was finished in 1891. The tall spires came later, to a different design, between 1926 and 1932. The central Moorhouse Spire reaches about 95 m, and the site is where Melbourne's first Christian service was held, in 1835.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the edge of Federation Square, facing the Flinders and Swanston Streets intersection. The cathedral is across Flinders Street to the north-west, about 170 m away, so face north-west.
